title: Private VPC egress handoff + KV-cache failure scenario walkthrough
summary: SE-led deep dive covering PrivateLink & NAT egress patterns, DNS resolution for interface endpoints, KV-cache warmup/failure handling, batching strategies under transient network loss, and mitigation playbooks. Agreed to run two lab tests: simulate hairpin NAT failure and measure tail latency with KV cache cold-starts; Redwood to provide runbook and a short benchmark harness.
topics: KV cache eviction and warmup scenarios

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-10 15:00 UTC
Duration: 1h15m
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Jordan (Acme), Maya (Acme Sec), Sam (Acme Infra)

[00:00] Alex Carter: All right everyone thanks for joining. We wanted to run through the egress and KV-cache failure scenarios today, make it practical. Priya will lead, I'll chime in on next steps.
[00:12] Priya Nair: Hey team, thanks. Quick agenda: PrivateLink / interface endpoints DNS behavior, NAT hairpinning and egress path, what happens to KV cache when the backend path drops, and then batching/quantization fallback strategies.
[00:27] Jordan Lee: Sounds good. for context our setup is two AZs, private subnets for inference, and a single NAT gateway in AZ-a, we also have interface endpoints for S3 and Secrets Manager, plus an internal NLB for model traffic.
[00:45] Maya Chen: Security note - traffic must not leave our VPC except to S3 via VPC endpoints. We have strict egress rules and logging requirements, SOC2 scope.
[01:02] Priya Nair: Understood. So first, PrivateLink / interface endpoints - generally the pattern we recommend is interface endpoints for management plane (secrets, s3, kms) and PrivateLink for control plane. One thing we see repeatedly is DNS split-horizon where resolver returns the private IP for endpoint in AZ-a, but cross-AZ traffic can be hairpinned through the NAT causing asymmetric paths.
[01:28] Sam Ortiz: We saw increased tail latency when the LB sent traffic to an instance in another AZ and the NAT had to hairpin back. We assumed the NAT was only for internet, but it ended up being the egress for some interface endpoints.
[01:45] Priya Nair: Right. In a scenario where the platform's inference runtime tries to reach a model artifact or a cache store through an interface endpoint and DNS resolves to a local ENI IP, if route table or SGs force traffic to go via NAT it introduces 1–2x tail latency. For high QPS workloads that can mean 50–200ms spikes.
[02:06] Jordan Lee: Is that the NAT gateway hitting the public elastic IP or internal? We use a managed NAT in the same AZ.
[02:14] Priya Nair: Managed NAT is fine but the hairpin cost is the problem. Also MTU shenanigans — sometimes PMTU discovery times out and you see fragmentation fallback. We recommend setting the MTU on the ENIs to match the NAT path or using path MTU consistent settings on the nodes.
[02:31] Maya Chen: On DNS, we've got Route53 resolver inbound/outbound endpoints for split-horizon. If the resolver mis-resolves an interface endpoint during failover, how does Redwood handle KV cache misses?
[02:44] Priya Nair: Good question. In our runtime, KV cache is primarily local in-node with a shared redis-like backing in the VPC by default. When a node loses connectivity to the backing store — say DNS goes wrong and the redis host resolves to a wrong IP — the runtime will mark the shared cache as degraded. We'll try local-only mode for a short tail period, flush pending requests, and then rehydrate once connectivity comes back. The tricky bit is cold-start behavior when many requests miss the local cache concurrently — you get thundering herd and model hot-shot cost.
[03:15] Sam Ortiz: We've observed that: weekend deploy and everyone hits a cold prefix, CPU and GPU utilization spikes, and tails go nuts. Any built-in mitigation?
[03:25] Priya Nair: Yes, Redwood runtime supports staggered cache warmup across pods via a lease / leader election so starts are pinned to a warmup window. But if the underlying DNS leads to intermittent connectivity, the lease can't be held and warmup fails.
[03:40] Jordan Lee: So if DNS flips to wrong private IP for an interface endpoint, do you fall back to hosted Redwood API? That's a security concern for us.
[03:50] Priya Nair: No automatic outbound fallback by default for Private deployments — we can enable a policy that allows fallback to dedicated-hosted only if you opt in and it's permitted by your security policy. Given Acme's requirements, we'd keep everything on VPC-only. We do, however, support a model-variant fallback where if a quantized variant is available locally we route to it to reduce token compute while the primary model is offline.
[04:15] Maya Chen: What's the impact on latency for model-variant fallback? If we switch to a q4_quant variant, is there a measurable increase in response distortion?
[04:26] Priya Nair: Typically quantized variants (8-bit, q4) show slightly different logits; for many use cases we see sub-point-one BLEU-like degradations for NLG tasks but the client perception is often acceptable. Latency improves significantly though — per-token cost drops 20–40% and per-request latency drops 10–30% depending on sequence length. We do recommend validating on a small eval set.
[04:50] Alex Carter: Quick interjection — Acme mentioned compliance. We'll attach our SOC2 and network design checklist after the call.
[04:59] Maya Chen: Please do. Also need to know about audit logs for egress events.
[05:06] Priya Nair: We emit detailed per-request traces that include route decision, KV cache hit/miss, and the egress path used. Those can be exported to your SIEM via Kinesis/Collector or s3 via interface endpoint.
[05:20] Jordan Lee: OK can we walk through the failure scenario we want to test?
[05:23] Priya Nair: Sure. Scenario A: AZ-b DNS resolver returns interface endpoint private IP in AZ-a, but route tables in AZ-b force traffic through a centralized NAT in AZ-a. Steps: 1) induce resolver stub to return cross-AZ IP, 2) run a 50 tps synthetic hitting cached prefixes while we disable connectivity briefly to the redis-like backing store. Measure p95/p99, model latency, and KV miss rates. Expected: tail latency increase and cache misses spike; with staging config we should observe lease renewal failures and local-only degrede behavior.
[06:02] Sam Ortiz: We'll need exact IPs and test harness.
[06:05] Priya Nair: We'll provide the harness — it's a small go client and a docker compose that runs our microbench with options to flip DNS and blackhole IPs. We'll send it after.
[06:17] Jordan Lee: How do you flip DNS? Our resolver is Route53 inbound endpoints that accept conditional forwarders.
[06:24] Priya Nair: In test we'll override /etc/hosts on the test nodes to simulate mis-resolve, or use a local dnsmasq in front of the resolver to return the cross-AZ IP. For a production-like test we'd configure Route53 resolver rules to forward to a test resolver that returns the chosen IP.
[06:39] Maya Chen: Are there recommended SG or NACLs to avoid hairpin?
[06:44] Priya Nair: Yes — prefer using endpoint-specific route table entries to ensure local ENI path stays local. Also assign ENIs in each AZ and ensure the service name resolves to AZ-local ENI IPs. For situations where NAT is needed, use a per-AZ NAT gateway to avoid cross-AZ hairpin.
[06:59] Jordan Lee: Got it. What about MTU? We saw fragmentation and PMTU discovery causing retries.
[07:06] Priya Nair: Two things: set node MTU to 1500 end-to-end if NAT involves encapsulation; or if using jumbo frames on substrate, ensure NAT supports them. Also ensure keepalive on connections to the cache store so TCP doesn't drop and induce reconnects under pressure.
[07:20] Alex Carter: Do we want to record these recommendations in the runbook?
[07:24] Priya Nair: Absolutely. Runbook will include: list of DNS test methods, expected metrics and dashboards, required IAM/SG changes, and steps to enable per-AZ NAT or move to interface endpoints properly.
[07:36] Jordan Lee: On the KV cache architecture — can you explain the eviction policy and how it interacts with local LRU? We have around 60GB per node for cache.
[07:47] Priya Nair: The runtime uses a two-layer cache: in-memory LRU per process for hot prefixes, plus a shared distributed store (redis/etcd-like). The eviction policy on the shared store is LFU-based with per-tenant namespaces. When network partitions occur, the node's in-memory LRU continues serving but misses to shared store increase. We delay expensive recompute by exponential backoff and jitter to avoid thundering herd. There's also an optional pre-warm hook that sequentially claims prefixes to compute.
[08:20] Sam Ortiz: In our initial POC you saw a big spike on cold starts. Is the sequential warmup something you can configure per-service?
[08:27] Priya Nair: Yes, warmup window and leader election TTL are configurable. For high-throughput setups we recommend a longer leader TTL to ensure one pod warms at a time. If leader election fails due to DNS network hiccups, the fallback is local-only with a capped QPS to reprotect the GPUs.
[08:44] Jordan Lee: What about batching — we aim for low single-digit ms latency, but some batching helps amortize GPU overhead. How does egress instability affect batching?
[08:54] Priya Nair: Batching increases tail exposure if network jitter is high. The runtime will lower max batch size and reduce wait window when p95 network latency crosses a threshold. There's an adaptive controller that monitors recent response times and reduces batch incentives to protect tails. That said, sudden cache misses (thundering herd) can fill batches with heavy requests, increasing GPU queueing.
[09:16] Maya Chen: Can we set hard SLOs to force fallback to smaller batch sizes?
[09:20] Priya Nair: Yes, you can pin batch size and latency SLOs in the route config; runtime will then prefer model variants and cache policies that honor those SLOs.
[09:29] Alex Carter: time check — 30 minutes in. Do we want to pivot to a quick walkthrough of the test harness?
[09:34] Jordan Lee: Yes please.
[09:36] Priya Nair: I'll share my screen; describing the harness: it's a go client with options --tps, --prefix-list, --dns-failure and a docker container that emulates the redis store and allows toggling blackhole for certain IPs. We also include a small tracer that logs per-request egress decision and cache state.
[09:58] Priya Nair: Example run: ./bench --tps 50 --prefix synthetic/high --duration 600 --dns-failure=hosts:10.0.3.5 which simulates interface endpoint resolving to 10.0.3.5 in AZ-a while test nodes are in AZ-b.
[10:20] Sam Ortiz: Will the harness produce a p99 histogram?
[10:23] Priya Nair: Yes, it writes out p50/p90/p95/p99 and a cache hit series. Also flamegraphs for CPU and GPU queue depth over time.
[10:33] Jordan Lee: If we flip DNS for a subset of nodes only, will the runtime notice and rebalance?
[10:39] Priya Nair: It depends — if only some nodes see different resolutions, those nodes will see a different egress path; load balancer will still route traffic based on health checks. We recommend making the change cluster-wide in the test to get consistent results.
[10:51] Maya Chen: Security question — when the runtime logs egress decisions, are IPs redacted?
[10:56] Priya Nair: We can redact IPs; by default we log resource identifiers and the decision outcome. Full IPs can be captured in a restricted audit stream if you need them.
[11:07] Alex Carter: Let's talk about model fallback. If the primary model becomes unreachable, what's the policy?
[11:12] Priya Nair: Policy options: 1) degrade to quantized variant locally, 2) re-route to a lower-capacity Dedicated pool in same VPC, or 3) if allowed, call hosted Redwood as last resort. For Acme we recommend option 1 + local capacity since hosted fallback violates data locality.
[11:30] Jordan Lee: Any way to replicate the quantization variance in a test to ensure QA acceptance?
[11:34] Priya Nair: We'll provide a small eval suite that runs both variants on a set of prompts and outputs diff metrics and example cases. It's part of the runbook.
[11:44] Sam Ortiz: We need to understand what metric thresholds you'd recommend for accepting a quantized fallback in production.
[11:50] Priya Nair: We suggest a two-tier gate: automated metric gate — e.g., less than 1.5% degradation on relevancy metric and less than 5% increase in hallucination rate on a pinned prompt set — plus a manual QA review for critical flows.
[12:07] Maya Chen: If we run these tests, will Redwood sign an SLA that covers egress path availability?
[12:12] Alex Carter: For Private deployments we can offer enterprise SLAs tied to dedicated capacity; egress path availability in customer's VPC is generally outside our SLA, but we do offer joint runbooks and support during remediation windows. We'll document that in the proposal.
[12:28] Jordan Lee: Good. Can we discuss logging granularity? p99 request logs could blow up storage.
[12:34] Priya Nair: We have sampling controls and can emit summary aggregates. For the run you'll want full traces, but in production we recommend 1% sampling with full capture on SLO breaches. Logs can be routed to your S3 via interface endpoints to keep traffic internal.
[12:49] Alex Carter: Any other network-level gotchas?
[12:52] Priya Nair: Two more: 1) asymmetric routing when using IGW + TGW across accounts — ensure return path stays in VPC otherwise health checks fail; 2) ephemeral port exhaustion on NATs under high QPS — per-AZ NAT reduces this and use of egress proxies with conntrack tuning helps.
[13:11] Jordan Lee: We did hit conntrack limits during our stress test. How do you recommend tuning?
[13:16] Priya Nair: Increase conntrack table size, and more importantly prefer keep-alive HTTP/2 multiplexed connections to the cache service to reduce ephemeral ports. Also tune OS-level tcp_tw_reuse and TIME_WAIT handling if permitted.
[13:30] Sam Ortiz: Are there any recommended kernel settings you ship with your node images?
[13:33] Priya Nair: Our hardened images include conntrack tuned, net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse=1, and tuned ephemeral port ranges. We'll share the AMI baseline.
[13:45] Jordan Lee: Back to testing: how long should we run the hairpin scenario to be meaningful?
[13:49] Priya Nair: I'd recommend 10–15 minutes at steady TPS to see stable p99 effects, then a 5–10 minute blackout to simulate transient outage, then recovery window. We look for delta in p95/p99 before/after and cache rehydration time.
[14:06] Maya Chen: For the blackout, do you recommend blackholing routes or toggling SGs?
[14:11] Priya Nair: Blackholing via iptables or route table is safest. SG toggles can cause connection reset noise that doesn't reflect real-world network partitions.
[14:21] Alex Carter: Time check — about 50 minutes left. Any objections to moving to runbook and timeline?
[14:26] Jordan Lee: No objections.
[14:28] Priya Nair: Runbook plan: 1) Prep (Jordan shares VPC artifacts), 2) Redwood provides harness + AMI baseline, 3) Dry run in staging with low TPS, 4) Full run with telemetry capture, 5) Postmortem and recommendations. We expect to complete steps 1–3 within one week.
[14:46] Sam Ortiz: If we find that shared redis store is the choke, can we switch to a sharded per-AZ store?
[14:52] Priya Nair: Yes, sharding by AZ reduces cross-AZ dependencies; we also support a local LRU with async replication which reduces sync penalties. But it increases complexity for global cache coherency.
[15:05] Maya Chen: We'll need a security review of the harness image and any keys it uses.
[15:10] Priya Nair: Of course — the harness uses ephemeral test creds and supports reading from your Secrets Manager via interface endpoint. We'll produce an SBOM and an image hash for verification.
[15:22] Alex Carter: Next steps recap: Priya sends runbook and harness + baseline AMI; Jordan shares VPC layout and route tables; Sam provisions test subnets; Alex schedules the lab.
[15:36] Jordan Lee: One last question — if we want to avoid NAT entirely, is moving everything to interface endpoints sufficient?
[15:42] Priya Nair: Mostly yes, but you need per-AZ endpoint ENIs and ensure DNS resolves to local ENI IPs. Also some services still require egress (external registries) where NAT will be needed; you can scope NAT only to those subnets.
[15:58] Maya Chen: Great. Thanks everyone.
[16:01] Alex Carter: Thanks, we'll follow up with the artifacts.
[16:05] End of transcript.
